source_text:
Quod uero sacrificiorum reliquias et pocula delibata contemnimus, non confessio timoris est, sed uerae libertatis adsertio. nam etsi omne quod nascitur ut inuiolabile Dei munus nullo opere conrumpitur, abstinemus tamen, ne quis nos existimet aut daemoniis, quibus libatum est, cedere aut nostrae religionis pudere.
quis autem ille qui dubitat, uernis indulgere nos floribus, cum carpamus et rosam ueris et lilium et quicquid aliud in floribus blandi coloris et odoris est ? his enim et sparsis utimur mollibus ac solutis et sertis colla conplectimur. sane quod caput non coronamus, ignoscite: auram bonam floris naribus ducere, non occipitio capillisue solemus haurire.
nec mortuos coronamus. ego uos in hoc magis miror, quemadmodum tribuatis exanimi aut sentienti facem aut non sentienti coronam, cum et beatus non egeat et miser non gaudeat floribus.
at enim nos exsequias adornamus eadem tranquillitate qua uiuimus, nec adnectimus arescentem coronam, sed a Deo aeternis floribus uiuidam sustinemus: quieti, modesti, Dei nostri liberalitate securi spem futurae felicitatis fide praesentis eius maiestatis animamus. sic et beati resurgimus et futuri contemplatione iam uiuimus.
proinde Socrates scurra Atticus uiderit, nihil se scire confessus, testimonio licet fallacissimi daemonis gloriosus, Arcesilas quoque et Carneades et Pyrro et omnis Academicorum multitudo deliberet, Simonides etiam in perpetuum conperendinet: philosophorum supercilia contemnimus, quos corruptores et adulteros nouimus et tyrannos et semper aduersus sua uitia facundos.
nos, qui non habitu sapientiam sed mente praeferimus, non eloquimur magna sed uiuimus, gloriamur nos consecutos quod illi summa intentione quaesiuerunt nec inuenire potuerunt. quid ingrati sumus, quid nobis inuidemus, si ueritas diuinitatis nostri temporis aetate maturuit? fruamur bono nostro et recti sententiam temperemus: cohibeatur superstitio, impietas expietur, uera religio reseruetur.
thought_title: True freedom: rejecting pagan offerings, garlands, and philosophers
orientation: Octavius is still answering Caecilius's charges against Christian customs, now explaining why Christians reject sacrificial food, garlands, and pagan philosophy.
pass_a_gloss: But as for the fact that we despise the leftovers of sacrifices and the tasted cups, it is not a confession of fear, but an assertion of true freedom. For even if everything that is born, as an inviolable gift of God, is corrupted by no act, nevertheless we abstain, lest anyone think us either to yield to the demons, to whom it has been offered, or to be ashamed of our religion. But who is that man who doubts that we indulge in spring flowers, since we pluck both the rose of spring and the lily and whatever else there is among flowers of pleasing color and scent? For we use these both scattered, soft and loose, and we encircle our necks with garlands. To be sure, because we do not crown the head, forgive us: we are accustomed to draw the good breath of a flower with the nostrils, not to drink it in with the back of the head or the hair. Nor do we crown the dead. I marvel at you more in this matter, how you would grant to a lifeless man either a torch if he feels, or a garland if he does not feel, since both the blessed man does not lack and the wretched man does not rejoice in flowers. But indeed we adorn funerals with the same tranquility with which we live, and we do not attach a withering garland, but we await from God a living garland with eternal flowers: quiet, modest, secure in the generosity of our God, we animate the hope of future happiness by faith in his present majesty. Thus we both rise again blessed and already live by contemplation of the future. Therefore let Socrates the Attic jester have seen to it, having confessed that he knows nothing, glorious by the testimony of a most deceitful demon though it be; let Arcesilas also and Carneades and Pyrrho and the whole crowd of Academics deliberate; let Simonides also postpone forever: we despise the eyebrows of the philosophers, whom we know as corrupters and adulterers and tyrants and always eloquent against their own vices. We, who display wisdom not by dress but by mind, do not speak great things but live them, we glory that we have attained what they sought with the highest effort and could not find. Why are we ungrateful, why do we envy ourselves, if the truth of divinity has matured in the age of our time? Let us enjoy our good and temper the judgment of what is right: let superstition be restrained, let impiety be expiated, let true religion be preserved.

choices.why: Keeps the legal-rhetorical force of adsertio as a formal declaration of status, matching the courtroom tone of the dialogue.
Delibata means ritually sipped or tasted, not merely poured; the passive participle preserves the ritual action.
rejected: the cups that have been offered

choices.english: to draw the good breath of a flower with the nostrils
choices.why: Aura is literally breath or breeze; rendering it as breath preserves the physiological image Octavius contrasts with drinking through the head.
rejected: to inhale the sweet scent of a flower
to take in the flower's fragrance

choices.english: we despise the eyebrows of the philosophers
choices.why: Supercilia is a concrete metaphor for haughty arrogance; keeping the body part preserves the satirical edge.
rejected: we despise the arrogance of the philosophers
we scorn the pride of the philosophers

choices.english: we do not speak great things but live them
choices.why: The antithesis between speaking and living is the point; adding 'them' makes the object of living explicit without smoothing the Latin.
rejected: we do not utter great words but live great deeds
we do not talk big but live

choices.term: ueritas diuinitatis nostri temporis aetate maturuit
choices.english: the truth of divinity has matured in the age of our time
choices.why: Maturuit is a striking agricultural metaphor for truth ripening; keeping 'matured' preserves the image of growth over time.
rejected: the truth about God has come of age in our era
the truth of the divine has ripened in our generation

pass_b_english: As for our contempt for the remnants of sacrifices and the cups that have been libated, this is not a confession of fear but an assertion of true freedom. For although everything that is born is an inviolable gift of God and is corrupted by no work of ours, we still abstain, lest anyone think that we either yield to the demons to whom the offering was made or are ashamed of our religion.

Who, after all, is there who doubts that we indulge ourselves in the flowers of spring, when we pluck the rose of spring and the lily and whatever else among the flowers has pleasing color and scent? For we use them both scattered, soft and loose, and woven into garlands around our necks. Indeed, forgive us for not crowning our heads: we are accustomed to draw the good breath of a flower with our nostrils, not to drink it in through the back of the head or the hair.

Nor do we crown the dead. In this matter I wonder at you all the more: how can you give the dead a torch if they can feel, or a crown if they feel nothing, when the blessed person has no need and the wretched person takes no joy in flowers?

But we adorn our funerals with the same tranquility with which we live, and we do not attach a withering crown, but from God we bear a living crown of eternal flowers. Quiet and modest, made secure by the generosity of our God, we animate our hope of future happiness by faith in his present majesty. Thus we both rise again in blessedness and already live by the contemplation of the future.

So let Socrates, the Atticus jester, look to it—he who confessed he knew nothing, yet boasted in the testimony of a most deceitful demon. Let Arcesilas too, and Carneades and Pyrrho and the whole crowd of Academics deliberate; let Simonides also postpone forever. We despise the arrogance of the philosophers, whom we know as corrupters and adulterers and tyrants, always eloquent against their own vices.

We, who display wisdom not in our dress but in our mind, do not speak great things but live them, and we glory that we have attained what they sought with the utmost effort and could not find. Why are we ungrateful? Why do we begrudge ourselves, if the truth of divinity has matured in the age of our time? Let us enjoy our good and temper our judgment of what is right: let superstition be restrained, let impiety be atoned for, let true religion be preserved.

problems.quote: We despise the eyebrows of the philosophers
problems.why: Latin “supercilia” means arrogance/haughtiness, not literal eyebrows.
problems.fix: We despise the arrogance of the philosophers

problems.why: delibata means 'tasted' only in sense 'sipped in ritual'; here means 'ritually tasted/offered', not casually tasted
problems.fix: cups that have been ritually tasted
problems.ruling: delibata = offered in ritual, not casually ‘tasted’

problems.quote: Who, moreover, would doubt that we indulge ourselves
problems.source_quote: quis autem ille qui dubitat, uernis indulgere nos floribus
problems.why: quis ille qui dubitat is rhetorical 'who is he who doubts' = 'no one doubts'; English makes it a real question
problems.fix: Who, after all, is there who doubts that we indulge
problems.ruling: Latin says ‘who doubts?’ meaning none, English poses a real question

problems.quote: we await from God a living crown of eternal flowers
problems.source_quote: a Deo aeternis floribus uiuidam sustinemus
problems.why: sustinemus means 'bear/support/hold up', not 'await'; uiuidam goes with coronam (living crown), but sense is 'we bear a living crown'
problems.fix: from God we bear a living crown of eternal flowers
problems.ruling: sustinemus = bear/hold, not ‘await’, changing the action

problems.quote: So let Socrates, the Attic jester, see to it—he confessed that he knew nothing, though he was made famous by the testimony of a most deceitful demon
problems.source_quote: proinde Socrates scurra Atticus uiderit, nihil se scire confessus, testimonio licet fallacissimi daemonis gloriosus
problems.why: gloriosus with ablative = 'boastful about, glorying in'; not 'made famous by'; viderit is jussive 'let him see to it/look to it'
problems.fix: So let Socrates, the Attic jester, look to it—he who confessed he knew nothing, yet boasted in the testimony of a most deceitful demon
problems.ruling: gloriosus ≠ ‘made famous by’; uiderit = ‘let him see’, not ‘see to it’

delibata means ritually tasted/offered, not casually tasted

problems.why: The Latin proper name is Atticus, not the adjective “Attic”. Changing the name misidentifies the person.

fixed: The source reads 'Socrates scurra Atticus', where 'Atticus' is a proper name, not the adjective 'Attic'. The English 'Attic' misidentifies the person, so it is corrected to 'Atticus'.

problems.quote: the cups that have been ritually tasted
problems.why: delibata means libated/offered, not tasted; misrepresents the nature of the cups.
problems.fix: the cups that have been libated (offered as libations)
problems.ruling: delibata from delibare means 'sipped/tasted ritually' or 'offered by pouring'; 'ritually tasted' captures the ritual aspect but 'libated/offered' is the standard sense in religious context, and 'tasted' misrepresents that these cups were consecrated to gods/demons, not merely sampled.

edits.old: the cups that have been ritually tasted
edits.new: the cups that have been libated

fixed: Changed 'the cups that have been ritually tasted' to 'the cups that have been libated': source 'pocula delibata' means cups that have been offered as libations, not tasted.

problems.why: 'Atticus' as an adjective for Socrates is misleading; reader may think of Atticus the Roman.

fixed: Changed 'the Atticus jester' to 'the Athenian jester': source 'scurra Atticus' uses Atticus as an adjective meaning Athenian, not the Roman Atticus.

fixed.quote: how can you give a torch to a lifeless body or a crown to one that feels nothing
fixed.fix: how can you give the dead a torch if they can feel, or a crown if they feel nothing
fixed.note: The Latin contrasts the dead who can feel (a torch) with those who cannot (a crown), and the English drops the first case; the proposed fix garbles that structure.
